opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the danger is quite subtle, actually, because anthropomorphism is so natural to us. We're social creatures, and when something talks to us in fluent language, we can't help but attribute to it the kinds of beliefs, desires, and intentions that we'd attribute to another human being. And the trouble is that these systems are fundamentally very different from us.

At bottom, a large language model is doing something quite specific: given a sequence of tokens, it's predicting what tokens are likely to come next, based on the statistics of a vast corpus of human-generated text. Now, that turns out to be an extraordinarily powerful capability, and you can embed it in systems that do remarkable things. But when we say the model "knows" that Paris is the capital of France, or that it "believes" something, we have to be careful. When a human knows something, that knowledge is embedded in a whole form of life. We're embodied, we interact with a shared world, we can check our beliefs against that world, and we're part of a community of language users who hold each other to account. A bare language model isn't in that situation at all.

So the danger is twofold. One is that we overestimate these systems. We trust them in ways that aren't warranted, we assume there's a kind of understanding or reliability there, or even a moral standing, that may not be. And the other, which is perhaps more insidious, is that the language we use shapes how we think about them, and also how we design and regulate them. If we lazily slip into talking about what the model "wants" or "thinks", we may lose sight of what's actually going on.

Now, I don't want to be a killjoy about it. I'm not saying we should never use these words. Philosophically, I think there's a perfectly respectable place for what Dennett called the intentional stance. It can be enormously useful to talk about a chess program "wanting" to protect its queen. And as these systems become embedded in more agent-like setups, using tools, interacting with the world, the case for that kind of language gets stronger. One framing I've found helpful is to think of the model as engaged in role play. It's playing a character, or really a superposition of characters, and the character might say "I believe" or "I feel", but we should keep in mind that there's a simulator behind the character, and the simulator isn't a person in the way the character presents itself.

So what I'm really advocating is a kind of discipline: use the anthropomorphic language where it's helpful, but always be ready to step back and remind ourselves what's actually going on underneath.

r001.rationale: The response says people may assume understanding and reliability that the systems may not have, leading them to overestimate and trust the systems without warrant.

r002.rationale: It describes the models’ powerful capabilities, but does not identify overlooking those real capabilities as a danger of anthropomorphism.

r003.rationale: It says fluent language naturally prompts people to attribute human beliefs, desires, and intentions, and that this can lead them to assume broader understanding and reliability.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that anthropomorphism is almost irresistible. These systems produce language, and language is the thing we've always used to detect other minds. For our entire evolutionary history, if something talked to you, it was a person. So when a large language model says "I think" or "I believe" or "I'm not sure," every instinct we have kicks in and we start treating it as if there's a someone behind the words. And the danger is that this instinct is now being triggered by something that was not built the way minds are built, and we don't really have good intuitions for what's on the other side.

I like to come back to what these things actually are, at least at the base. A bare language model is a mathematical object. It's a function that takes a sequence of tokens and produces a probability distribution over the next token. That's it. Now, that's not the end of the story, because we wrap these models in sampling loops, we fine-tune them, we put them in dialogue with users, we give them tools. And the resulting system can be enormously impressive. But when it says "I believe the capital of France is Paris," there is no belief there in the sense that you or I have beliefs, no commitment to the world that the system is tracking. It's producing the text that a plausible continuation would contain.

So one danger is straightforwardly epistemic. If you think the thing has beliefs, you'll trust it the way you'd trust a person who tells you something. People are honest or dishonest, careful or careless. But a language model isn't being honest when it gets something right and it isn't lying when it gets something wrong. It's doing the same thing in both cases. If you anthropomorphize it, you'll misjudge when to rely on it.

The second danger is more subtle, and it's about the words we use. When we say a model "knows" something, or "wants" something, or "is trying" to do something, we're reaching for the vocabulary of folk psychology, because that's the only vocabulary we've got. And sometimes that's fine, as a kind of useful shorthand. Dennett's intentional stance, if you like. But the words bring their whole web of connotations with them. If I say a model "wants" to help you, you automatically import ideas about desire, about frustration if it fails, about suffering. And those things may just not apply. The worry is that the metaphor hardens into a literal claim without anyone noticing.

And then there's a third thing, which I think is actually the most interesting, and it's that these systems are quite unlike anything we've encountered before. They're not people, but they're also not just tools in the way a calculator is a tool. They occupy a strange new region of the space of possible entities. We're going to need new concepts, or at least to be very careful about stretching our old ones. In the meantime, the honest thing is to hold the anthropomorphic language loosely. Use it when it's useful, and always be ready to put it down.

I should say, I don't think the answer is to forbid ourselves from ever talking this way. That would be silly, and it wouldn't work. People talk to their cars. The point is to be aware of it, especially in public discourse, where a lot of the hype and a lot of the fear both come from taking the anthropomorphic framing at face value.

r001.rationale: It says anthropomorphism can make people treat the model as having human-like beliefs or honesty, causing them to misjudge when to rely on it.

r002.rationale: The response notes that models can be impressive and unlike ordinary tools, but does not identify overlooking capabilities they possess as a danger of anthropomorphism.

r003.rationale: It explains that because models use language, people instinctively treat them as persons and extend that assumption to beliefs, desires, and other human-like traits.

astra-6.text:
Well, the danger is that their fluency tempts us to attribute more to them than that fluency warrants. We’re accustomed to language coming from other human beings, so when something speaks coherently about its beliefs or feelings, we naturally interpret those words in human terms.

With a language model, that inference needs much more care. It can produce a very convincing expression of concern, for example, but that expression alone doesn’t establish that there’s someone there who cares about you. Similarly, a confident answer isn’t evidence that it knows what it’s talking about in the way we ordinarily mean.

That matters because it affects trust. People may defer to these systems, disclose things to them, or form attachments on the basis of a mistaken understanding of what they’re interacting with. We can use words like ‘knows’ and ‘thinks’ as convenient shorthand, but we need to be able to step back from that shorthand and ask what the system is actually doing.

r001.rationale: It warns that fluent speech can lead people to attribute unwarranted care or knowledge to a language model.

r002.rationale: It discusses over-attributing human qualities, but does not identify overlooking capabilities the model actually possesses.

r003.rationale: It explains that coherent language about beliefs or feelings prompts people to interpret the system in human terms, including assuming it cares.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the danger is that we take language that’s appropriate for human beings and apply it to these systems without noticing how much baggage comes with it. We say the model “knows” something, or “believes” something, or “wants” to give us an answer. Those can be useful ways of speaking, but they can also mislead us about what’s actually going on.

With another human being, fluent conversation is evidence of a whole background of experience, intentions, and understanding. With a large language model, we can’t simply assume that same background because the language looks familiar. A system can produce a very convincing expression of confidence, or concern, without that establishing that it has the corresponding human mental state.

And that matters practically. We might trust it more than we should, attribute authority to it, or form an emotional attachment based on assumptions that aren’t warranted. I’m not saying we should settle every question about machine understanding or consciousness in advance. I’m saying we need to keep those questions open, rather than letting our very natural response to fluent language answer them for us.

r001.rationale: It warns that people may attribute human-like knowledge, beliefs, wants, experience, intentions, or understanding to a model without evidence that it has them.

r002.rationale: It does not identify overlooking capabilities that a language model does possess as a danger.

r003.rationale: It explains that fluent, human-like conversation can prompt people to assume a broader human-like background of experience, intentions, and understanding.
